plan.contextChunk: This figure shows a two-lens telescope system consisting of a convex objective lens (lens 1, on the left) and a concave eyepiece lens (lens 2, on the right), with the distances f1 and f2 indicated by horizontal brackets beneath the optical axis. Two parallel input rays enter from the left at a small angle δᵢ relative to the optical axis; lens 1 bends them toward the objective focal point to the right of lens 2, and lens 2 then diverges the rays so they exit as a parallel bundle at a larger angle δₒ. The blue vertical marker d shows the offset of the shared focal point from the optical axis in the shown Galilean afocal geometry, where the objective focal point aligns with the eyepiece focal point. This figure demonstrates how a Galilean-style telescope achieves angular magnification equal to the ratio f1/f2 by manipulating ray angles through the two-lens arrangement.

interactionPlan.concept: A Galilean telescope achieves angular magnification by pairing a convex objective with a concave eyepiece, spaced so their focal points align, bending incoming parallel rays into a steeper parallel exit bundle.
elements: Horizontal optical axis line (blue)
Lens 1: convex lens symbol (tall, tapering), labeled 'lens 1' above it
Lens 2: concave lens symbol (shorter, flared ends), labeled 'lens 2' above it
Top ray path (thick purple line): enters from left, refracts at lens 1, refracts at lens 2, exits right
Bottom ray path (thin light-purple line): enters parallel to top ray, refracts at lens 1, refracts at lens 2, exits parallel to top ray
Dashed light-purple line extending from the bottom ray between the lenses to the focal point behind lens 2
Blue dot marking the shared focal point where the rays from lens 1 would converge
Vertical black line with arrows labeled 'd' measuring the distance from the optical axis to the blue focal dot
Arc marker and label 'δ_i' indicating the angle between the top input ray and the horizontal
Arc marker and label 'δ_i' indicating the angle between the bottom input ray and the horizontal
Arc marker and label 'δ_o' indicating the angle of the exiting rays relative to the horizontal
Horizontal dimension bracket labeled 'f_1' under the system, spanning from lens 1 to the vertical plane of the focal dot
Horizontal dimension bracket labeled 'f_2' under the system, spanning from lens 2 to the vertical plane of the focal dot

interactions.label: Objective focal length (f₁)
interactions.teaches: Increasing the objective lens's focal length pushes the focal point further away, requiring a longer telescope tube but increasing the angular magnification ratio (f₁/f₂).

interactions.label: Eyepiece focal length magnitude (f₂)
interactions.teaches: Decreasing the eyepiece's focal length brings Lens 2 closer to the focal point, causing the exiting rays to bend more sharply and thus increasing the magnification.

interactions.label: Input ray angle (δ_i)
interactions.teaches: Changing the angle of the incoming rays causes the exit angle to change proportionally, demonstrating that the angular magnification ratio δ_o/δ_i remains constant for the given lenses.

interactions.label: Lens 2 defocus offset
interactions.teaches: Moving the eyepiece away from the ideal afocal separation (f₁ - f₂) misaligns the focal points, causing the exiting rays to converge or diverge instead of remaining perfectly parallel.

demo_steps.title: Afocal magnification
demo_steps.narration: In a properly focused Galilean telescope, parallel input rays exit strictly parallel. The magnification is the ratio of the output angle to the input angle, governed by the focal lengths.

demo_steps.title: Changing input angle
demo_steps.narration: Observe how a larger input angle results in an even larger output angle. The vertical offset 'd' at the focal point increases, but the ray paths remain parallel upon exit.

demo_steps.title: Increasing magnification
demo_steps.narration: Increasing the objective focal length (f₁) relative to the eyepiece (f₂) yields a much higher exiting angle (δ_o), providing greater magnification.

demo_steps.title: Defocusing the system
demo_steps.narration: Shifting the eyepiece away from the exact difference of the focal lengths (f₁ - f₂) ruins the afocal alignment; the exiting rays are no longer parallel, creating a blurry image.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The telescope scales up the angle of incoming light by exactly the ratio of the two lenses' focal lengths (f₁/f₂), provided the lenses are separated by exactly the difference of those lengths.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Ensure the optical ray-tracing logic perfectly matches the geometry: rays enter at angle δ_i, pivot at the vertical center plane of lens 1 toward a focal point at distance f₁ from lens 1. They intersect lens 2 (positioned at f₁ - f₂ + offset). If offset is 0, they exit lens 2 exactly parallel to each other at angle δ_o. The vertical offset 'd' is simply f₁ * tan(δ_i). Keep the color palette clean: blue for the axis/focal dot, black for lenses/brackets, varying weights/opacities of purple for the rays.

plan.authoredInteractions:
- Sliders for focal lengths f₁ and f₂: update all ray paths through both lenses and display the angular magnification ratio δₒ/δᵢ = f₁/f₂ in real time, with the lens separation adjusting to maintain the shown Galilean afocal configuration
- Drag the input ray angle δᵢ to change the angle of the two parallel input rays and see the output angle δₒ change proportionally, with ray traces updating through both lenses
- Drag lens 2 along the optical axis to deviate from the shown afocal separation (f₁ - f₂, using the positive bracketed distances), showing the exit beam become converging or diverging and the blue focal-point offset d shift relative to lens 2

authoredContext: A small change in the input ray angle gives a larger change in the output ray angle. The magnification of the telescope is the ratio, $M$, of the angular deviation of an output ray, $\delta_o$, to the angular deviation of an input ray, $\delta_i$.  Writing the focal point offset, $d$, in terms of the rays passing through the centers of lenses 1 and 2 gives the relation, $M = f_1/f_2$, where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are the respective ray focal lengths.
